title: Scheduler heuristic jitter causing attention index desynchronization and stochastic softmax drift
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Intermittent correctness regression observed after merging the adaptive scheduler heuristic that reorders prefill -> decode handoffs for throughput gains. Under medium-to-high batching with long context (>2048), requests occasionally observe small, reproducible shifts in token probability mass (KL divergence ~1e-4 to 1e-3 vs baseline) that accumulate over generation and manifest as subtle token drift and rare token duplication. Root cause hypothesis: non-deterministic ordering (scheduler jitter) across worker shards can change attention index allocation timing for competing kernels, which in turn allows slightly different softmax numerics and cache slot races to surface. This ticket tracks the investigation, mitigation, and rollout of a correctness-first fix while preserving as much of the scheduler perf win as possible.
steps_to_reproduce: Deploy runtime-1.19 with adaptive scheduler enabled (feature flag scheduler.adaptive=true) on a 4-GPU dedicated shard pool.
Run the long-context generation harness against Open-Llama-7B with seq_len_prefill=3072 and batch=8 using the provided perf-prom load generator (scripts/test/harness/prefill_long_context.sh).
Collect token-level logits for 5000 requests and compute average KL divergence to a deterministic baseline (scheduler.adaptive=false) using tools/analysis/kl_compare.py.
Observe KL in the 1e-4..1e-3 range for a reproducible subset (~0.6% of traces) and rare token duplication in 0.05% traces.
Enable verbose runtime tracing (RUNTIME_TRACE=1) and capture scheduler decision traces and kernel-selection logs for a failing trace ID.
Correlate the trace with GPU-side prefetch ordering logs (perf/kern_log) to see inconsistent ordering between prefill and decode kernels across adjacent steps.
observed_behavior: Small but consistent KL divergence vs deterministic baseline under long-context batched prefill workloads.
Occasional token duplication or off-by-one token sequences in generated output for affected traces.
Trace logs show different kernel-selection ordering and differing timing of attention map materialization across shards.
No immediate GPU OOMs or crashes; correctness-only regression but visible in downstream QA fuzz tests and customer eval prompts.
hypothesis_and_findings: Adaptive scheduler adjusts priority using a lightweight spectral-cost estimator which intentionally perturbs ordering to improve tail latency. The perturbation is non-deterministic across workers.

Prefill -> decode handoff assumes deterministic ordering when reusing KV cache slots and handshake fences; jitter breaks that assumption and produces micro-timing differences during softmax reduction.
Numeric drift is amplified by long sequences because small per-step softmax differences compound, increasing KL over many tokens.
We observed subtle race windows where a worker would prefetch a kernel result while another shard updated a shared slot index; timing differences led to stale reads in a handful of traces.
steps_taken: Added additional logging to scheduler decision path and kernel-selector (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1824).
Built targeted unit test that drives deterministic scheduler ordering and stress test for the prefill handshake (tests/scheduler/test_stable_handoff.py).
Reproduced failure locally in CI containerized repro with sleep/noise injection to simulate production jitter (trace ID: trace-20251115-41A7).
Temporarily gated the heuristic behind runtime feature flag and rolled the flag to 20% canary for further telemetry collection.
Collected perf telemetry showing a 4.2% p99 throughput improvement when heuristic is enabled but with correctness regressions in a small fraction of traces.
proposed_fix: Introduce sequence-stable ticketing: attach monotonically increasing handshake sequence numbers to prefill requests so that kernel-selection and KV slot reuse are ordered deterministically at the shard level.
Make the scheduler perturbation deterministic per-request by seeding the spectral-cost noise with request-id hashed seed (preserves perf variation but removes cross-worker nondeterminism).
Add an atomic fence around KV slot handoff where feasible to eliminate stale-read window (micro-bench to measure cost).
Backfill regression unit tests that assert token-level equivalence for a canonical seed under noisy scheduling.
tradeoffs_and_risks: Atomic fences and additional sequencing add a measurable overhead: estimated 2.5% throughput regression in worst-case microbench; p50 unaffected.
Making perturbation deterministic reduces exploration potential of the heuristic—may lower some tail improvements but keeps correctness intact.
Complexity increase in scheduler code path; requires careful code review and e2e testing to avoid deadlocks or priority inversion.
next_steps: Implement deterministic-perturbation + handshake-sequence prototype in branch fix/eng-997001 (owner: Mateo).
Run full regression suite and long-context perf harness across dedicated 4-GPU and hosted canary pools (timeline: 3 days).
If prototype passes correctness and perf thresholds (KL < 1e-5, p99 throughput regression <3%), prepare PR and coordinate rollout with SRE and PM for gradual enablement.
If overheads exceed thresholds, iterate on a hybrid approach: only enable atomic fences on race-prone kernel families (investigate via kernel-level tagging).
Draft postmortem-style notes for internal runbook and add a diagnostic flag to surface handshake-sequence mismatches in live logs for future incidents.
